To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hyperglycemic, not hyperlipidemic, db/db mice have impaired beta-cell glucose sensing and that this is accompanied by changes in beta-cell gene expression, which can be normalized by phlorizin treatment.
chronic hyperglycemic exposure is sufficient to cause the loss of beta cell differentiation, which can be reversed by lowering blood glucose levels, and that this loss is not due to hyperlipidemia.
chronic hyperglycemic exposure, independent of plasma lipids, is sufficient to cause a progressive loss of beta-cell glucose sensing and differentiation in the db/db model of diabetes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular events that lead to beta-cell dysfunction in diabetes.
the mechanisms by which chronic hyperglycemic conditions lead to beta-cell dysfunction in type 2 diabetes.
the mechanisms of beta-cell dysfunction in diabetes and the identification of new approaches to prevent or reverse beta-cell dysfunction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic hyperglycemic conditions are sufficient to cause a loss of the specialized beta-cell phenotype and that this is not a result of hyperlipidemia in the db/db mice.
chronic hyperglycemic exposure is sufficient for beta-cell loss in db/db mice, and that the loss is not dependent on plasma lipid levels.
chronic hyperglycemic stress is sufficient to induce beta-cell dysfunction, and that the loss of beta-cells is not the result of a primary defect in these cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the loss of beta cell function is due to a loss of beta cell differentiation.

chronic hyperglycemic exposure, independent of lipid changes, is sufficient for a global alteration of beta-cell gene and protein expression, which is associated with the progressive loss of beta-cell glucose sensing and secretory function.
chronic hyperglycemic conditions, such as those seen in type 2 diabetes, are sufficient to induce a loss of beta-cell identity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hyperglycemic conditions, rather than hyperlipidemia, are responsible for the loss of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in db/db mice.

chronic hyperglycemic stress is sufficient for the progressive loss of beta-cell function in db/db mouse islets and that the normalization of GIIS is not necessarily accompanied by a complete normalization of beta-cell gene regulation.
chronic hyperglycemic exposure is a major factor in the pathogenesis of beta-cell failure.
